title: Are Your Questions Working For You — Or Against You?
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: This article demonstrates through a paired classroom scenario how the quality of an opening question determines the depth of student thinking — not the talent of the teacher or the ability of the students. Using a scene from the children's novel Poppy, Lippert contrasts a closed retrieval question ('Who can tell me what happened?') against an open interpretive question ('Why does this moment matter so much?') and shows how the latter pulls all 18 students into genuine thinking while the former allows most to opt out. The author identifies the structural features that make a strong question: it must create thinking rather than test recall, it must belong to everybody rather than the handful who always raise their hands, and it must carry enough interpretive weight that even a quiet student has something real to contribute. The article also addresses question-rescue moves — how to help stuck pairs think rather than simply answering for them. Lippert argues that the quality of student thinking is often determined long before the discussion begins, in the moment the teacher selects a question.
points: The quality of student thinking in a discussion is largely determined before the discussion begins — it lives in the question the teacher chooses to open with, not in what happens after.

A weak retrieval question ('Who can tell me what happened?') creates a passive majority while a handful of students do all the thinking; a strong interpretive question ('Why does this moment matter?') makes thinking unavoidable for all 18 students.

Strong questions must belong to everybody: they should carry enough interpretive weight that quiet students and reluctant participants have something real to contribute, not just the few who always raise their hands.

Turn-and-talk structures amplify strong questions dramatically — the same three minutes produces fundamentally different results depending entirely on whether the question had one right answer or genuinely demanded thinking.

A teacher's rescue move for stuck pairs should prompt independent thinking ('How would you feel if...?') rather than providing the answer — sustaining productive struggle rather than short-circuiting it.
quotes: The quality of student thinking is often determined long before the discussion begins. It starts with the question we ask. A weak question lets students hide. A strong question makes thinking unavoidable.

The teacher stands at the board and asks, 'Who can tell me what happened in our reading yesterday?' Maybe five or six of the usual hands shoot up. The teacher calls on one student to answer... Three minutes. A handful of kids did the thinking. The rest sat back and watched.

The room erupts. All 18 kids talking at once. The teacher moves through the desks, crouching down, listening... The answers are richer, more connected, more alive than anything one raised hand could have given her.

But here's the part that matters most. It wasn't just the kids who got called on who did the thinking. It was all 18 of them. The quiet ones. The ones who've learned to wait it out because someone else always answers. Not this time. The question belonged to everybody.

It wasn't talent — both teachers know their kids and their curriculum. It was the question, and the structure around it. The first question had one right answer. If you remembered it, you were in. If you didn't, you sat there.
She crouches down: 'How would you feel if you had to go talk to the bully who just hurt your best friend?' That's all they needed. 'Oh, she's probably shaking. She won't want to look at him.'
